sections.text: A dog year is not seven human years. The dog age calculator on this site gives two estimates: an epigenetic formula, human age = 16 x ln(dog age) + 31, which applies to dogs of 1 year and older, and a traditional stepwise rule that counts the first year as 15, the second as 9 and every later year as 4. For a 5-year-old dog the formula gives 56.8, the stepwise rule gives 36 and the old multiply-by-seven rule gives 35. The estimates disagree most for young dogs, which is exactly where seven times is least useful.
All figures below are human-year equivalents computed with the formulas stated above, rounded to the nearest tenth where needed. ln is the natural logarithm.
Where the epigenetic formula comes from

The formula comes from a 2020 paper in the journal Cell Systems by Wang and colleagues in Trey Ideker's group at the University of California San Diego. The researchers looked at DNA methylation, chemical tags on DNA whose pattern shifts as an animal ages, in about 100 dogs that were almost all Labrador retrievers (published summaries give 104 or 105 dogs). They aligned the dog patterns with human methylation data and fitted a single curve. The result is a logarithm, which means aging runs fast early and slows later.

The university's own announcement flags a limitation: the clock was built on a single breed, and some breeds are known to live longer than others. Treat the output as an estimate of molecular age for a typical Labrador-like dog, not a measurement of your particular dog.
How fast does the curve slow down?

Each extra dog year adds 16 x ln((n + 1) / n) human years, so the gain shrinks steadily. The second year adds 11.1, the third 6.5, the fifth 3.6, the tenth 1.7 and the fifteenth 1.1. The epigenetic line crosses the multiply-by-seven line at about 9.6 years: before that, seven times is too low, and after it, seven times runs above the formula. From about 14.4 years on, the stepwise total is higher than the formula's, because the stepwise rule keeps adding a flat 4 per year while the formula keeps slowing.

A rescue dog is estimated to be 6 years old. Multiplying by 7 gives 42. The stepwise rule gives 15 + 9 + 4 x 4 = 40. The epigenetic formula gives 16 x ln(6) + 31 = 16 x 1.792 + 31 = 59.7. The first two are within two years of each other, and the formula is roughly 18 to 20 years higher. None of them is wrong arithmetic. They answer different questions: the stepwise rule tracks developmental milestones, while the formula tracks molecular aging against humans.
For a puppy of 9 months (0.75 years) the calculator uses the traditional method only, 0.75 x 15 = 11.25 human years, and shows no epigenetic figure.

items: Using the logarithmic formula for puppies. Below 1 year it breaks down: at 0.25 years it gives 8.8, and at 0.1 years it gives -5.8, which is meaningless. That is why the calculator limits it to dogs of 1 year and older.
Applying the formula to cats. The calculator uses the stepwise rule for cats, because the epigenetic fit was built from dog data.
Reading one number as a diagnosis. A human-equivalent age says nothing about whether your dog is healthy for its age. Weight, teeth, joints and breed all matter.

Ignoring size and breed. The calculator asks for a size band (small under 9 kg, medium 9 to 23 kg, large over 23 kg) because it uses size to choose a life stage label, but the human-age formula itself is the same for every size.

Assuming a precise result. Lifespans differ between breeds, so the same chronological age can mean a very different stage of life for a Great Dane and a Chihuahua. This post does not give breed-specific tables because the source study does not support them.

sections.text: This is an educational estimate, not veterinary advice. Questions about screening, diet, exercise or changes in behavior should go to your veterinarian, who can judge your dog as an individual.
